text: In this town, every clock skips exactly one minute at 11:59 PM. Nobody knows why. Every night, clocks jump straight from 11:59 to 12:01. The locals have learned to live with it, but everyone follows one strange rule: never look outside during the missing minute. I thought it was ridiculous until one night when I saw someone standing outside my bedroom window. It was a little girl, probably around seven years old. She was completely still, staring directly at me. Something about her face felt familiar, but I couldn't figure out why. I immediately checked my clock, 11:59. I blinked, and suddenly it was 12:01. The girl was gone. The following night, I saw her again. This time she was standing at the end of my driveway. I opened the front door and called out to her, but she didn't move. Instead, she slowly raised her hand and pointed toward the old house across the street. She disappeared. So I decided to investigate the house that night. It had been abandoned for years, but something about it seemed strangely familiar. Inside, I found an old grandfather clock standing against the wall, but something was wrong. The grandfather clock wasn't showing 12:01. It was showing twelve o'clock, the missing minute. Its pendulum was still swinging, even though every other clock in town had already moved forward. I stepped closer, trying to understand what I was looking at. Nearby, I found an old music box sitting on a dusty table. I wound it up, and it started playing a melody I somehow recognized. Suddenly, I heard a little girl's voice behind me. "You still remember?" I turned around. There she was. I asked her who she was and why she kept following me. She just smiled and said, "You promised you'd never forget." Before I could respond, I heard another voice coming from behind the staircase. A little boy stepped out. "Do you still remember us?" I backed away, completely confused. Then more children began appearing from the hallways. Some were sitting on the stairs, while others stood quietly beside the walls. One of them finally spoke. "In here, it's always twelve." I looked back at the grandfather clock. "Why are you all here?" A little girl looked down before answering. "This is the only place where forgotten children can still exist." Another child stepped forward. "You're the only one who can still remember us." I didn't understand what they meant until an old photograph had slipped out from behind the music box and landed on the floor. I picked it up. It showed a group of children standing together in front of the very same house, and standing right in the middle was me. I looked younger, maybe six or seven years old. Beside me was the little girl from my window. Suddenly, memories came rushing back, the games we played, the music box, the promises I made. She wasn't a stranger. She was my little sister.
